title: Stream processing
summary: Stream processing is a programming paradigm that treats sequences of events in time as the central input and output of computation. It simplifies parallel software and hardware by restricting the kinds of parallel computation possible, applying kernel functions to each element in a stream. The paradigm is especially suited to applications with high compute intensity, data parallelism, and data locality, such as image, video, and digital signal processing. Systems use streaming algorithms, stream management systems for distribution and scheduling, and hardware acceleration via floating-point units, GPUs, and FPGAs. Code examples demonstrate continuous SQL queries joining data streams and complex event detection from event sequences.

mechanisms.title: Stream abstraction and kernel functions
mechanisms.explanation: The paradigm views data as unbounded, continuous sequences of events. A series of kernel functions is applied to each element in the stream. Kernel functions are typically pipelined, and the programming model exposes data dependencies, allowing compiler tools to automate and optimize on-chip management tasks.

mechanisms.title: Stream management and hardware acceleration
mechanisms.explanation: Software stacks include stream management systems for distribution, scheduling, and query languages. Hardware components provide acceleration through floating-point units, GPUs, and FPGAs. Streaming algorithms trace parallel processing for data streams, and hardware techniques such as scoreboarding initiate DMA when dependencies are resolved.
